first_impression.reaction: Unusual. The intro admits most guides 'cite no one' and promises to say which bits are sourced and which are just folklore. That's exactly what I want, so I kept going and checked whether they actually did it. Mostly they did.

journey.quote: we have been plain about which details come from UNESCO, the Smithsonian or parish sources and which are simply often told.
journey.reaction: Good. Separating sourced fact from family lore is the first thing I'd check, and they've told me up front they'll do it.

journey.section: The formal asking and the engagement
journey.quote: We found no official or academic source for them in our research, so what follows is how families often tell it.
journey.reaction: Honest about the limits of their research. I trust the rest more because of this line.

journey.section: The kavor and kavorkin, the wedding godparents
journey.quote: The kavor (godfather) and kavorkin (godmother, often the kavor's wife) are often told to be the couple's sponsors for life
journey.reaction: 'Often told' comes up a lot in this section and the next one. It's honest, but after the fifth or sixth time it reads like a verbal tic. Fine, just a bit repetitive.

journey.quote: It asks couples to make contact at least eight months ahead and to confirm the priest and church before booking anything else.
journey.reaction: A concrete number and a practical order of operations. This is the kind of detail I'd actually put in a spreadsheet.

journey.quote: One parish says the sacrament must follow the canons of the Armenian Apostolic Church
journey.reaction: Which parish? 'One parish' and 'another' in the US. I'd like to know who so I can check it. Small point, it's still better than nothing.

journey.section: Lavash, honey and the broken plate at the door
journey.quote: UNESCO inscribed "Lavash, the preparation, meaning and appearance of traditional bread as an expression of culture in Armenia" on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2014.
journey.reaction: Year, body and a link I can click. Checkable. Good.

journey.quote: updated 17 June 2026, sets the overall level at Level 2, "Exercise a high degree of caution", and Level 4, "Do not travel", within 5 km of Armenia's border with Azerbaijan
journey.reaction: Dated, sourced and not sugar-coated. A travel company telling me the risky bits without being asked is a point in its favour.

journey.quote: male dual nationals aged 18 to 28 may be liable for military service.
journey.reaction: That's a real catch most glossy guides would bury. Flagging it is the opposite of hiding things.

journey.section: Civil registration and the church wedding
journey.quote: We could not read an official Armenian source on this.
journey.reaction: Admits a gap instead of guessing. I'd rather this than a confident wrong answer.

journey.section: Marrying in Armenia as Australians: the legal steps
journey.quote: You will have a single point of contact, with the fee agreed in writing before any work begins; the legal and church paperwork stays with you, the registry and your priest.
journey.reaction: Fee in writing up front and a clear line on what they don't do. That's the right instinct. But 'the fee' of what, calculated how? And do they take a cut from the venue? Not answered.

journey.section: Planning the day around your family's traditions
journey.quote: Every Armenian family carries its own version of these customs, and the best weddings make room for the ones that matter most to yours.
journey.reaction: Soft close, a bit of warm fluff after a very factual piece. Harmless.

unanswered_questions: Do you take a commission or mark-up from venues and suppliers, or is your fee the only thing you earn?
What does the Wedded Advisor fee actually cover, and how is it calculated (flat, percentage, tiered)?
Have you actually run a wedding in Armenia, or an Armenian-Australian wedding? Show me one with the real budget.
Which US parishes are the parish rules quoted from?

turn_offs_found.quote: Every Armenian family carries its own version of these customs, and the best weddings make room for the ones that matter most to yours.
turn_offs_found.why: 'The best weddings' is the only bit of unsupported, feel-good language in the piece. Minor, but it stands out against how careful the rest is.

would_share_with: My fiancee, mainly for the Smartraveller and dual-national military service section

cta_reaction.quote: If you would like one person to coordinate the venue, travel and suppliers around those answers, [speak with a Wedded Advisor](/wonderland-concierge?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=armenian-wedding-traditions).
cta_reaction.why: It comes after the evidence, not before, and 'fee agreed in writing' is the right signal. I'd click through to the concierge page to look for the fee model and whether they take a cut. I wouldn't enquire from this page alone, but I didn't expect a traditions article to answer that.

top_3_changes: Name the parishes behind the 'one parish' and 'another' rules (or link them) so the claims can be checked.
Cut back on 'often told'. Say it once per section as a label rather than in nearly every sentence.
Replace 'the best weddings make room' with something plain and factual to match the rest of the piece.

open_questions.question: Fee model and commission questions are business details deferred per orchestrator; treat as not must-fix for this post.

assumptions: Daniel is reading out of general interest or a partner's heritage; the persona card does not state an Armenian background, so relevance is scored low-moderate.
Absence of prices is the house standard and not penalised, per orchestrator.
